questions.q: Which six functions make up the capstone simulator core, and which earlier course concept does each one directly implement?
options: initState (basis states), applySingleQubitGate (index-pairing from Lesson 24 applied to Chapter 2 gates), applyCNOT (Chapter 3's CNOT generalized), GATES (the fixed gate matrices), probabilities (the Born rule), and simulateShot (Lesson 26's shot sampling)
Six unrelated utility functions with no connection to earlier lessons
Only initState and applyCNOT; the other listed pieces are optional extras not used in validation
A single function that does everything, with no modular structure
questions.explain: Each piece of the core is a direct, traceable implementation of a specific earlier-course idea — the point of the capstone is showing that the whole course's math reduces to exactly these six small, composable functions.

questions.q: Why was the Bell-state circuit (H then CNOT on |00⟩) specifically chosen to validate the capstone simulator core?
options: Because its correct result, (|00⟩+|11⟩)/√2, was already independently derived by hand in Chapter 3, so running it through the new core and matching that known answer is a genuine correctness test
Because it is the only circuit the core is capable of running
Because Bell states always produce a different result every time they're computed, making any output 'correct'
Because it requires no gates at all, making it trivial to check
questions.explain: A simulator can only be validated against results you already trust independently. Reusing the Chapter 3 Bell-state result (derived by hand) as the target answer is exactly how the lesson confirms the new code is actually correct, not just running without errors.

questions.q: The real node run of the Bell-state circuit through the capstone core produced the final state [0.7071, 0, 0, 0.7071], probabilities [0.5, 0, 0, 0.5], and 2000 simulated shots giving counts of 1004 and 996 (not exactly 1000/1000). What does this combination of results demonstrate?
options: The exact state vector and probabilities confirm the gate logic is correct, while the shot counts (close to but not exactly 1000/1000) confirm the sampling function correctly reproduces the finite-sampling behavior described in Lesson 26
The simulator has a bug, since repeated shots should always produce an exact 1000/1000 split for a true 50/50 probability
The probabilities are wrong because they don't match the shot counts exactly
Only the state vector matters; the shot counts are irrelevant to validating the core
questions.explain: The exact state vector and probabilities test the deterministic gate-application logic, while the near-but-not-exact shot split (1004/996) is exactly the expected behavior of finite random sampling around a true 50/50 probability, consistent with what Lesson 26 already established.

questions.q: What is explicitly missing from this capstone core compared to a production simulator like Qiskit's Aer or Q#'s simulator?
options: Full complex-amplitude arithmetic (needed for gates like Y, S, T, and rotations), performance optimizations (multi-threading, GPU acceleration), noise models mimicking real hardware, and gate decomposition into a device's native gate set
Nothing — this core is functionally identical to Qiskit's Aer simulator in every respect
The ability to apply any gates at all
The concept of a state vector, which production simulators don't use
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that the core demonstrates the same fundamental architecture as production tools (state vector, index-pairing, shot sampling) but deliberately omits the engineering needed for full gate coverage, performance at scale, and realistic noise modeling.

questions.q: Why can an S gate (from Chapter 2, matrix [[1,0],[0,i]]) not be correctly added to this specific core's GATES object and run through applySingleQubitGate as written, even though H, X, and Z work fine?
options: Because applySingleQubitGate and the state array only handle real numbers, but S's matrix entry i is an imaginary number — correctly supporting it requires changing the state representation to track real and imaginary parts, not just adding a new matrix
Because applySingleQubitGate only works for exactly 2-qubit systems
Because the S gate cannot be represented as a 2x2 matrix
Because GATES is a fixed object that cannot have new entries added to it in JavaScript
questions.explain: H, X, and Z all happen to have purely real matrix entries, so they work fine with the real-valued arithmetic in this core. S (and Y, and the rotation gates) require genuine complex arithmetic, which this deliberately minimal core does not implement — exactly the gap the lesson's closing section and Check Yourself question point to.
